A model that prices every player's chance of scoring, alongside the bookmaker's own number for the same player — and an honest account of how often it has been right.

What survives every measurement

Backing every priced player returned -28.7% a bet. Taking only the ones we rate above the price returns -19.6% — the model's ordering is worth 9.1 points, and still 2.1 points of implied probability short of breaking even.

Best is the best price any archived book posted, and Shop is what that is worth in points of implied probability — the one edge here that does not need the model to be right. Band is what every bet at that price returned across the whole population, vetoed players included: context for reading a row, never the reason it is on the list.

Tracked — fade the overpriced (a lay, not a bet at a book)

Unproven at a real price — the measurement is strong and the venue is the question. in the band where the market's own bias pays, players we rate under a third of the book's number scored 2.61% against a 6.92% de-vigged price over 690 bets: laying at fair is +62.5% [+44.3, +79.4]. The control: a permutation keeping prices, outcomes and weeks and shuffling only which player we called overrated never reached the real best cell in 200 draws (p = 0.000); the market's own bias gives +37.7% at the median, ours +72.7%. Out of sample: positive in all three seasons and strengthening: +40.6%, +45.7%, +49.8% at the -2pt cut. What is untested is a fill: it carries 4.63% of margin on the No decimal, which a Yes quote would have to be half again above fair to spend. The open question is not the spread but whether a venue lists it at all — see lay_sheet.

Who scores, not what to bet

This board ranks players by how likely they are to score. Its top pick is right 51.6% of the time against 16.2% for a candidate drawn at random — about 3.2x the field, over 849 backtested games (2023-2025). Restricted to picks it rates above 0.50 it reaches 60.9% [56.7%, 64.8%], on 45% of games.

Against the bookmaker, same 849 games (2023-2025). The honest yardstick — a price, not a coin flip.

A different window from the accuracy strip above. That pools every retrained fold; only the seasons with archived prices can be set against a book, so these 849 games are a subset. The two Top-1 figures on this page are not the same measurement and are not subtractable.

UsThe bookDifference
Top-151.6%52.7%-1.1 pp
Top-383.3%83.3%+0.0 pp
Top-593.6%92.6%+1.1 pp

We are behind the book on Top-1 by 1.1 points and ahead on Top-3 and Top-5. Read that as it is: this model brackets the scorer better than the price does and isolates him worse. If you want one name, the book's favourite is still the better single guess; the board earns its keep on the shortlist.

It is not a bet card. Backing its top 3 at the prices actually posted returned -7.8% [-12.1, -3.6] across 849 backtested games — the market is priced ahead of it. Use the ranking to decide who is likely to score; do not size a position on the edge columns.

The 25 best two-leg combinations of the top 4 in every game on the slate, ranked by expected value. Built from the 27 strongest of the 64 eligible players, which is enough to find them: every number here is a product of the legs', so a slip using a weaker leg cannot outrank 25 built without it.

Legs are multiplied as if independent. Re-measured on 1,698 team-games of backtest residuals, teammates' outcomes correlate -0.024 — sharing a scoring game and competing for the same touchdowns very nearly cancel — so the correction would be smaller than the error in measuring it. 1 of these rows put more than one leg in the same game — the Game column says how many games a slip spans, and a long one nearly always doubles up somewhere. Their price is arithmetic, not a quote: a book prices its own correlation into a same-game parlay and will come back shorter. The strip above is this exact setting replayed over 2023-2025: 1,593 slips, of which 16.7% landed against the 17.1% we said beforehand. The Expected on $100 column below is still a forecast rather than that measurement.

Parlay

Pick players and back every combination of them — a full cover, not one slip. n players is 2ⁿ − 1 slips, so one is a single bet and five is 31. The table below is what each number of scorers returns.

Only the backable half is a bet. A cover multiplies whatever edge each leg carries, so it multiplies that half — not the average of the two, which is higher because the fade side is sharper.

31 slips on 5 players — every combination: 5×1-leg · 10×2-leg · 10×3-leg · 5×4-leg · 1×5-leg — at $1.00 each, $31.00 staked. All 5 legs priced by the book.

Breakeven is 4 of 5 — and that happens 40.7% of the time, with the measured teammate correlation of -0.024 applied.

Returns vary within a row because the legs are priced differently — two of five can be the two short legs or the two long ones. The figure shown is weighted by how likely each combination is.

Expected result -$3.97 (-12.8%) against -$1.58 (-5.1%) for the same $31.00 on the 5 singles alone. A cover is leverage on the edge in each leg: per dollar a single returns e and a k-fold returns (1+e)^k − 1. These prices leave a negative edge, so multiplying them pays the margin once per leg and the cover loses harder than the singles do. Only a better price or a better probability fixes that; the structure cannot.

Graded. Replayed over 66 weeks (2023-2025) at $1.00 a slip on the prices actually posted, this rule returned between -22.4% and -1.2% depending on pool size, and no pool size had an interval clearing zero. 5 of 6 returned less than the same money on the singles — which is what a negative edge per leg does when it is multiplied: a k-fold pays the margin k times. At the 5 you have picked it returned -10.6% [-30%, 11%] with 19 of 57 weeks ahead.

Would a different rule have helped? Over the same 66 weeks, ranking by the model's own number instead of the blended one returned +19.0% at 4 players against -12.9% — ahead at 4 of 6 sizes. No interval clears zero, and the best of 44 random orderings reached +274% on the same weeks — so read this as a direction, not a result. Blending pulls our number toward the price, which is what makes it better calibrated and also what deletes the disagreement a bet lives on.

By team

Which side scores first is a true coin-flip question, and the model beats the coin: AUC 0.674 over 2,278 walk-forward team-games, calibrated from 6% to 94%. Bookmaker says is the same split read off their own first-TD prices, and it is blank for a game they have not priced yet — most of the slate, early in a week. Expected touchdowns is the fitted team rate; shut-out risk is the chance of no offensive touchdown at all.

The groups below were fitted on 2015–2023 — the seasons the model trains on — using 71,070 rows that passed the same activity filter production uses. Everything measured about them is measured on 2024–2025, 18,210 rows the grouping never saw. Fitting and scoring on the same rows is how a segmentation invents a pattern.

Who scores, not what to bet

This board ranks players by how likely they are to score. Its top pick is right 17.0% of the time against 3.8% for a candidate drawn at random — about 4.4x the field, over 849 backtested games (2023-2025).

Against the bookmaker, same 849 games (2023-2025). The honest yardstick — a price, not a coin flip.

A different window from the accuracy strip above. That pools every retrained fold; only the seasons with archived prices can be set against a book, so these 849 games are a subset. The two Top-1 figures on this page are not the same measurement and are not subtractable.

The 25 best two-leg combinations of the top 4 in every game on the slate, ranked by expected value. Built from the 27 strongest of the 64 eligible players, which is enough to find them: every number here is a product of the legs', so a slip using a weaker leg cannot outrank 25 built without it.

Legs on this market always come from different games, so multiplying them assumes only that separate games are independent of each other. Same-game slips are left out entirely: one player scores a game's first touchdown, so two legs from one game cannot both land. The strip above is this exact setting replayed over 2023-2025: 1,548 slips, of which 1.1% landed against the 2.2% we said beforehand. The Expected on $100 column below is still a forecast rather than that measurement.

Parlay

Pick players and back every combination of them — a full cover, not one slip. n players is 2ⁿ − 1 slips, so one is a single bet and five is 31. The table below is what each number of scorers returns.

Only the backable half is a bet. A cover multiplies whatever edge each leg carries, so it multiplies that half — not the average of the two, which is higher because the fade side is sharper.

Breakeven is 2 of 5 — and that happens 22.4% of the time, with the measured teammate correlation of -0.046 applied.

Returns vary within a row because the legs are priced differently — two of five can be the two short legs or the two long ones. The figure shown is weighted by how likely each combination is.

Expected result -$7.29 (-23.5%) against -$2.36 (-7.6%) for the same $31.00 on the 5 singles alone. A cover is leverage on the edge in each leg: per dollar a single returns e and a k-fold returns (1+e)^k − 1. These prices leave a negative edge, so multiplying them pays the margin once per leg and the cover loses harder than the singles do. Only a better price or a better probability fixes that; the structure cannot.

Graded. Replayed over 66 weeks (2023-2025) at $1.00 a slip on the prices actually posted, this rule returned between -66.9% and +52.7% depending on pool size, and no pool size had an interval clearing zero. 5 of 6 returned less than the same money on the singles — which is what a negative edge per leg does when it is multiplied: a k-fold pays the margin k times. At the 5 you have picked it returned -31.1% [-56%, -2%] with 16 of 57 weeks ahead.

Would a different rule have helped? Not by re-ranking: this market's blend does not move the number, so the model's own ordering and the published one pick the same players at every size. Of 44 rules tried over 66 weeks, none has an interval clearing zero.

By team

Which side scores first is a true coin-flip question, and the model beats the coin: AUC 0.674 over 2,278 walk-forward team-games, calibrated from 6% to 94%. Bookmaker says is the same split read off their own first-TD prices, and it is blank for a game they have not priced yet — most of the slate, early in a week. Expected touchdowns is the fitted team rate; shut-out risk is the chance of no offensive touchdown at all.

The groups below were fitted on 2015–2023 — the seasons the model trains on — using 71,070 rows that passed the same activity filter production uses. Everything measured about them is measured on 2024–2025, 18,210 rows the grouping never saw. Fitting and scoring on the same rows is how a segmentation invents a pattern.

Biggest group first. Sorted by return instead, a group of sixty with one lucky longshot in it would lead the page.

On the dashed line, the probability matched what happened. Above it, the type scored more often than either of us said; below it, less. Filled markers are ours, hollow ones the bookmaker's — where a hollow marker sits further from the line than the filled one beside it, we described that type better than the price did.

Built 19 September 2026 from the project's own dashboard — every figure on this page is computed by the same code that serves the live app, then frozen into this file. Nothing here updates on its own; rebuild to refresh it.

Probabilities are estimates, and the profitability figures describe a replay at closing prices in past seasons. No bet in them was ever struck. Nothing here is advice.
